content:

New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) is celebrating the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) coming into force today, “bringing New Zealand wine improved access to one of the world’s fastest-growing economies”.

NZW said the agreement gives New Zealand wine brands greater confidence to build their presence in India, with tariffs reducing progressively over the next decade.

The FTA also includes a ‘Most Favoured Nation’ commitment for wine. If India agrees more favourable tariffs for wine in a future FTA with another country, eligible New Zealand wine will automatically receive the same tariff treatment. In addition, the FTA includes a dedicated ‘Annex on Trade in Wine, Whisky and Other Distilled Spirits’. NZW explained it aims to facilitate trade through “greater transparency, regulatory cooperation and clearer treatment of wine-specific issues” as well as establish “a working group on topics such as technical matters, labelling and certification”.

Improved access under the FTA is expected to make the market increasingly attractive to exporters. Depending on the wine’s value, tariffs on eligible New Zealand wine will reduce over ten years from 150% to either 50% or 25%.

New Zealand wine exports to India have “historically been modest, but they grew 48% in the last year to just under NZ$438,000”.

India’s wine market is largely concentrated in three cities: Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru. Together, those cities account for half of the country’s wine consumption and are home to around 70 million people. This is a market 13 times the size of New Zealand and is comparable to the United Kingdom.

Red wine accounts for a significant share of imported wine to India, “creating opportunities for a range of New Zealand wine styles alongside Sauvignon Blanc”. NZW said sales of wine are also growing. In the year to March 2026, Maharashtra (of which Mumbai is the capital city) sold a record 13 million litres, or around 1.4 million cases, while imports grew 14% by volume in 2025.

Together, the organisation believes these trends create a significant opportunity for New Zealand’s wine exporters.

“We thank Ministers and officials for their work to secure improved access to a market with considerable long-term potential”, said NZW CEO Anishka Jelicich.

“By working to bring the FTA into force quickly, the Government has ensured that New Zealand will also benefit from the Most Favoured Nation preferential tariff rates that have been negotiated under the EU India FTA. Those tariff reductions are more substantial and would not have been available to us if the EU deal had entered into force first.

“India remains largely untapped for New Zealand wine, so our focus is on helping our members assess the opportunity through practical market intelligence and insights, connections with key stakeholders and opportunities in-market to build their brands,” she said.

New Zealand Winegrowers recently hosted India’s only Master of Wine, Sonal C Holland, as a keynote speaker at its annual Wine Business Forum in Wellington. Her message to the audience was clear; the FTA removes a significant barrier, but long-term success in India will require commitment, patience and strong local relationships.

“Next month, we look forward to working with New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (NZTE) at ProWine Mumbai. The major international trade fair will include a 20 strong contingent of businesses showcasing New Zealand wine to the Indian trade. These types of events are incredibly valuable for our members, helping them to build distributor relationships and a pipeline in a growing premium segment,” said Jelicich.

title: Judging under way at the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show
summary:
More than 550 wines will be presented before the judges this week as tasting for the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show gets underway at Marlborough Events Centre. From Wednesday 21 to Friday 23 October, chief judge Stu Marfell will be joined by shadow chief judge Murray Cook to lead a team of ten senior judges and six associate judges, including guest judges Jennifer Docherty MW from Hong Kong and long-time international wine judge Terry Copeland, through the tasting. Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October, with trophy winners announced at the Marlborough Wine Show Celebration on Friday 13 November 2026.

content:
Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October and trophy winners announced Friday 13 November. Image supplied

More than 550 wines will be presented before the judges this week as tasting for the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show gets underway at Marlborough Events Centre.

From Wednesday 21 to Friday 23 October, chief judge Stu Marfell will be joined by shadow chief judge Murray Cook to lead a team of ten senior judges and six associate judges, including guest judges Jennifer Docherty MW from Hong Kong and long-time international wine judge Terry Copeland, through the tasting.

“We’re lucky to have two guest judges who bring real breadth to the table,” said Marfell.

“Jennifer has a truly global palate and a sharp sense of how Marlborough wines sit on the international stage, and Terry has been judging here and overseas for more than 30 years. Their perspective alongside the deep local knowledge of our panel is exactly the balance a regional show needs.”

Jennifer Docherty is one of around 420 Masters of Wine worldwide, and the first ethnically Chinese and Mandarin-speaking MW. Based in Hong Kong, she has spent more than 16 years as a wine buyer and educator across the UK, Hong Kong and mainland China. She now works as an educator, a judge and a wine communicator who has chaired a judging panel at the IWC Sake Competition in London for a decade.

Terry Copeland has judged wine competitions for more than three decades across New Zealand, London, San Francisco, Sydney and Tokyo. After a career in wine sales, marketing, export and supply chain, he went on to lead NZ Young Farmers and Federated Farmers, and is now Programme Director, Export Growth at the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Organisers said entries cover the full range of Marlborough wine styles, with growth in several classes this year. Sweet wine entries have almost doubled, the Sauvignon Blanc aged one year or older category is up and so is the current vintage regional blend Pinot Noir.

“It’s great to see more aged Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir coming through,” Marfell said.

“These styles work to showcase the depth and breadth Marlborough has to offer, as well as the confidence producers have in how their wines develop over time.”

The Legacy Trophy, which awards the wine with the highest scores for three vintages within a ten-year period, will be judged solely by the chief judges and guest judges today (20 October), before judging gets into full swing tomorrow.

QuayConnect is once again the show’s naming sponsor with general manager Jaron McLeod saying the company is proud to continue its support.

“Marlborough wine is one of the top of the south’s great export stories, and much of it moves through our supply chain on its way to the world,” he said.

“Backing a show that recognises the skill and care that goes into every bottle is a natural fit for QuayConnect.”

Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October, with trophy winners announced at the Marlborough Wine Show Celebration on Friday 13 November 2026.

content:
The winery castle at All Saints Estate. Image credit Griffin Simm

KIN Restaurant at All Saints Estate has been awarded a Chef’s Hat in The Age Good Food Guide 2027, its third hat since opening in January 2023, with a score of 15/20.

Described by the guide as having “dishes shaped by a restless creativity”, the award recognises KIN’s “commitment to regional produce, quality and exceptional dining”.

Set within the heritage listed 19th-century castle at All Saints Estate on the banks of the Murray River, KIN is led by executive chef Jack Cassidy.

His menus showcase seasonal produce from local growers and the estate’s own gardens and vineyards, with an “inventive use of native ingredients, matched with wines from All Saints Estate, St Leonards Vineyard and Mount Ophir Estate”.

Owners said the hat reaffirms KIN as one of Australia’s destination dining venues and that its setting within a winery is what makes it unique.

“Nick, Angela and I are incredibly proud to see KIN awarded a hat in The Age Good Food Guide 2027. It’s wonderful recognition for Jack and the team, who create dishes that reflect the seasons, our gardens and our connection to the region,” said Eliza Brown, director at All Saints Estate.

“This award would not be possible without our loyal guests and the hard work, passion and creativity of our team.”

Cassidy said the recognition is “for the team”.

Every day we work with what the region and our own gardens give us, and to have that recognised by The Age Good Food Guide means a great deal to every one of us,” he said.

First published in 1979, The Age Good Food Guide “remains the benchmark for dining in Victoria”.

summary:

content:
The second installation of a two-part opinion piece by Edward Cavanagh that concludes a cautionary tale: understanding what motivated China to adopt the position it did in relation to Australia, and how the subsequent fight played out, should dampen any optimism about the re-emergence of the Chinese market for the wine industry.

In 2019, China was Australia’s largest trading partner, representing more than a quarter of its total trade balance. And Australian wines made up a small but significant chunk of this figure, accounting for over a billion dollars’ worth of exports per year.

A great market had opened up.

But then a great market would disappear – and the importance of certain positions adopted by the Australian government in this saga should be highlighted.

“A market of over a billion dollars per annum became a market of a few hundred thousand bucks per maybe-once-every-now-and-then-let’s-see.”

 

We poked the panda

The Australia-China relationship had episodically experienced some stress-testing throughout 2018 and 2019, the biggest years of climbing export growth for the wine industry, over a number of issues. These included statements made by Foreign Minister Julie Bishop between March and July of 2018 about maritime security in the South China Sea, followed by the federal government’s announcement (and only the day before Turnbull was ousted) on August 23rd 2018 that Huawei’s 5G network would not be approved for rollout in Australia. There were also repeated allegations from late 2017 right up to mid-2019 of government interference (mostly through some pretty questionable political donations and a number of reports that Chinese spies had been planted in parliaments and universities).

But the real deterioration of the relationship came with the outbreak of COVID-19 and Prime Minister Scott Morrison’s early response to the pandemic.

Specifically, the People’s Republic of China took offence to a series of public announcements by Morrison throughout April and May of 2020, which were reiterated in a speech before the UN General Assembly in September 2020, about the need for an independent probe into the Chinese origins of the COVID-19 outbreak. This involved providing the World Health Organisation with what Morrison called ‘weapons inspector-style powers’ in Wuhan. Throughout these months of lockdown and uncertainty, Morrison arrogated to himself the responsibility of engaging in something of a diplomatic campaign by zoom conference, in which he attempted to drum up international support for an intervention by calling into question the truthfulness of Chinese reporting about the outbreak and its early spread – remarks that he was unafraid to make repeatedly in press conferences in Australia at this time.

Whatever the clarity or the opacity of the reporting of Chinese health authorities about the outbreak of coronavirus, Morrison’s COVID-19 campaign came a little too close, for the PRC’s liking, to an allegation of responsibility for the global economic turmoil that the pandemic had wrought.

When, in August 2020, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce announced that it would be investigating the impact of current trading arrangements on the economy, Australia’s diplomatic lines to China had already run cold. It did not help that, within just weeks of the Chinese investigation into trade getting up and running, the Australian government resolved to join a UN chorus in condemning China’s treatment of Muslim Uyghurs in Xinjiang and political dissidents in Hong Kong.

Confirming a provisional decision reached in November 2020, which came in the context of a few knee-jerk quarantine restrictions, a formal announcement followed from Beijing on March 26th 2021 that the export market for Australian wine was no more.

But the imposition of trade barriers at the Chinese end did not simply come through a new blanket tariff, as Angus Colovic has explained in his treatment of the topic. The official determination by the Chinese Ministry of Commerce found that Australian exporters had been guilty of ‘dumping’ their wines into the Chinese market.

Now this was World Trade Organization parlance for the practice of undercutting domestic producers through unfair competitive advantage. Whatever the increase in area under vine that China witnessed in these years, it was hardly the case that the Chinese grape and wine sector had grown to become anywhere near the size of Australia’s, or any other of the many nations who sought entry into this lucrative market, leaving aside whatever their own regulations permitted around quality and blending material for Chinese-produced wines for its domestic market.

Still, the logic of the determination was clear enough. And it was expressed in a way that all of the trade lawyers could well understand as they licked their lips, even if they disagreed about the consistency of this decision with the general tenor of entire libraries full of WTO general agreements. Whatever they could or could not do about it, the reality was that China’s anti-dumping laws kicked in with immediate effect. Even with ships on the water, they kicked in. Overnight, the duties imposed on Australian wine in containers of 2L or less landed anywhere between 116% and 218%, with the earliest reports indicating a blanket imposition of 200%. The dragon had snorted.

There are two striking features when it came to the imposition of these duties. One was the sheer scale of them. The other was the abrupt rapidity of them. And Australian wines were suddenly and immediately nowhere near capable of reaching the Chinese market at a competitive price point as a result of them.

Some of this wine had to be discounted to achieve at least some return; a lot of it was warehoused; a bit of it went into the black market; a good deal of it just sat on cargo ships destined either to return to Australia for relabelling or otherwise disposal. Some shipping insurers paid out; others didn’t.

A disaster like this only had one parallel in history: and that is when the UK had rather hastened to join the European Economic Community in 1973 without forewarning any of their Commonwealth trading partners about the consequences that this would inevitably entail for supply chains that had been mostly linked up in the Victorian era. Quantitatively, the scale of the volte face in China was of much greater magnitude than this, however. Millions of litres were destined for the Chinese market. And overnight this wine needed to find another home – mostly, alas, in storage. A market of over a billion dollars per annum became a market of a few hundred thousand bucks per maybe-once-every-now-and-then-let’s-see.

These measures targeted bottled wine.

Altogether separately, but around the same time, the movement of bulk wine into and around China was subject to new customs regulations, which required registration, more paperwork, compliance to new standards, and stricter labelling requirements, in addition to new restrictions imposed on the receiving entity.

In other words, whereas Australian bottled wine was priced out of the Chinese market through tariffs, Australian bulk wine could only ever make it into an increasingly competitive market wrapped in layers of red tape that meant higher costs and greater uncertainty both for exporters and importers.

Widely seen as a retaliation against the Morrison government’s remarks about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic, there are other facets to the Chinese loosening of its embrace of Australian wine that are probably worth considering in a way that isn’t unhelpfully woebegone.

Such facets should certainly mitigate against any optimistic belief that the Chinese market for Australian wine will somehow magically return someday soon to the glory years of 2016–2020, and should probably have mitigated against the uninhibited optimism that was shown towards the foreverness of the market in the first place.

For starters, Chinese people were beginning to drink less in this period. And per capita alcohol consumption in China has continued to fall ever since. White collar professionals in the cities were simply no longer totally writing themselves off at work events as they once did. Lavish banquets were already apparently becoming less frequent even before coronavirus. What’s more, cultures around gift-giving were also beginning to shift. Bottles of big red wine with big red labels became big red flags. Little and little remained in this world apart from a reverence for fine wine more so as a cake to have rather than a cake to eat. Penfolds would always do well in this market; Penfolds counterfeits would surprisingly do even better. Aside from luxury wines, what Australia had been flooding the Chinese market with were cheapish big-bodied red wines, sometimes with more than a bit of residual sugar, and which were sometimes bottled up with labels all flashy with orientalist iconography – and these were only ever going to enjoy a temporary moment in the rising sun with so much of this new sociocultural smog settling into the cityscape.

If history is anything to go by, then Australian wine exporters would eventually have discovered this for themselves, albeit far too late, and then instinctively geared themselves up to discount their ways out of trouble, like they did with just about every other market crisis. But in China they never got the chance. Its government’s anti-dumping measures, which are still widely seen by analysts and commentators as an exertion of China’s power of economic coercion, caught everyone off-guard.

“And I rather hope that some of the marketing masterminds who are paid by winery businesses, like those who are paid out of industry levies, consider more fulsomely the geopolitical context of the world that was shaken up by the Global Financial Crisis of 2008-2010 before they plug into any overseas market again, let alone a market so fickle, tricky, twisted, and cunning as China’s.”

 

Enter the trade lawyers

Australia put up a fight using the World Trade Organization (WTO) dispute settlement system.

The first step required Australia to invite China to participate in bilateral negotiations for sixty days, which it did on June 22nd, 2021. But since there was no agreement at the end of this period, Australia was entitled to ask the WTO Dispute Settlement Board (DSB) to establish a panel to consider whether or not arbitration was appropriate. In the meantime, both parties, China and Australia, made it clear that they wished to advance their own cases in this forum, and agreed to a common procedure for arbitration in December 2021. When a new standalone panel was established in March 2022, both of the parties overloaded it with ‘voluminous evidence’, such that an extension had to be agreed to the process.

And then even more evidence kept rolling in!

Come August, the Chair of the panel had to report to the DSB that the evidence was indeed so ‘voluminous’ that a determination would not be delivered in 2022. A month later, the Chair clarified that in fact the panel did not expect to issue a report to the parties before mid-2023.

That brings us to October 30th, 2023, when the Chair of the panel informed the DSB that the panel report was finished and scheduled to be circulated to Members on November 10th, 2023. But no report was ever delivered because, on the same day, the Chinese team and the Australian team announced that they were in a position to settle the dispute away from the WTO, and therefore jointly requested the panel to suspend its work until March 31st, 2024.

That’s right, a two-year-long exercise in paying for lawyers to develop a complex argument over 46 separate articles of the WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement, 38 separate articles of the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, and even four articles of the true classic in the multilateral genre, the General Agreement on Tariffs Trade, resulted in thousands of pages of evidence about the wine trade but no report.

That the Australian submissions were overwhelmingly more serious, and likelier to earn a determination in Australia’s favour, seems a reasonable enough conclusion to reach. Unwishful of attracting any further political attention towards their strategies of economic coercion that were becoming increasingly notorious on the world stage, the PRC did not want a ruling that could jeopardise any of its activities here and elsewhere, current or planned; it wanted a deal. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was invited to Beijing for talks with President Xi Jinping in early November 2023, and wine was right at the top of the agenda, above even lobsters, visas, and iron ore.

Few people can entirely know what goes behind closed doors of this kind, but it seems plausible that Albanese received assurances from Xi Jinping that China would restart imports of lobster and review the tariffs on wine, if in return Australia committed to a formal withdrawal of its case before the WTO panel.

This outcome was confirmed, when, on March 29th, 2024, both parties announced to the WTO that they were discontinuing their case. Later, on June 17th, 2024 – three and a half years after the provisional ban on Australian imports of bottled wine was announced – a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade of Australia was signed in Canberra and Beijing.

“The Chinese government’s anti-dumping measures, which are still widely seen by analysts and commentators as an exertion of China’s power of economic coercion, caught everyone off guard.”

 

Open sesame…again?

China was open for trading again.

But there was a problem.

Citizens of the PRC never rediscovered their appetite for Australian wines after 2025 to the extent they were quaffing them before 2021.

One wonders whether or not it would have been better for the wine industry to have seen a WTO determination instead of this outcome. Alas, it does not matter now.

The point to remember here, and in the context of the findings presented in my previous article on this topic, is that Australia was outdone. And I rather hope that some of the marketing masterminds who are paid by winery businesses, like those who are paid out of industry levies, consider more fulsomely the geopolitical context of the world that was shaken up by the Global Financial Crisis of 2008-2010 before they plug into any overseas market again, let alone a market so fickle, tricky, twisted, and cunning as China’s.

As with sundry other Chinese experiments that involve playing around with foreign economies, the PRC has played such a beautiful long game over the past two decades. They are arguably the only ones who know how to mix economic coercion with diplomatic mind-games to play one convincingly, and the sheer size of their market, coupled with the supreme level of control the PRC enjoys over its own institutions, provide them a commanding power to dominate whenever they choose to play it.

Australian wine was but a pawn, but it is unlikely to have had any role at all in the Chinese masterplan were it not for the Hawke-era reforms on tariffs, tax, and industry protections that were responsible for putting the sector into exactly this position.

I am not for a moment suggesting that those reforms were a bad thing. They were right for the time and right for Australia.

Still, we are allowed to feel upset by the ways in which globalisation and free trade were sold to neoliberal economies on a set of presumptions that China, through its might and power, has subsequently unsettled; one might also pause in this frame to consider equally the EU’s subsidy system, New Zealand’s eligibility for WET rebates, and the Trump tariff regime, alongside Chinese economic coercion, and reconvene with the same scepticism.

If free trade supposes an openly competitive arena whereby everyone takes their cues from the market, then the experience of the Australian wine industry both at home and abroad, and especially when it comes to China, shows that this arrangement has not always played out all that reciprocally or fairly. Australia got smashed, but it did not impose massive reverse tariffs on Chinese goods coming into Australia; it took the principled route instead to the WTO. What it got was four years of uncertainty, and the re-emergence of a market that was hardly as big or as lucrative for the vast majority of producers as it was before the walls came down.

No export-oriented national wine industry should ever place all of its eggs into this basket again, but South Africa recently has, and others probably will.

Australia looks like it might again too. But should it?

content:
Rachel McBryde has taken over the role following Sam Berketa’s ten-year tenure. Image supplied.

For the first time in a decade, McLaren Vale winery Alpha Box & Dice has a new head winemaker.

Rachel McBryde, who joined the business in 2024, steps into the role following Sam Berketa’s ten-year tenure, bringing “international experience, a passion for lesser-known varieties and a fresh perspective to its ever-evolving Alphabet of Wine”.

Her career has taken her around the world, from Marlborough in New Zealand to Napa Valley and Ontario in North America. McBryde also spent five years working across d’Arenberg and Gemtree in McLaren Vale, explored sparkling winemaking in the Adelaide Hills and spent three years in Coonawarra at Katnook Estate and Penley Estate, working with some of Australia’s most celebrated Cabernet Sauvignon.

“What drew me to Alpha Box & Dice was a love of the weird and wonderful,” said McBryde.

“The Alphabet of Wine and its focus on lesser-known varieties is something that really interests me. In Australia, we have this incredible freedom to grow varieties from Burgundy alongside those from Piedmont or the Mosel and develop our own interpretations of what those grapes can be in a new environment. That’s exciting, and it’s what we do at Alpha Box & Dice.”

Built around the idea of creating an entire ‘Alphabet of Wine’, Alpha Box & Dice approaches each letter as a different winemaking project, exploring new varieties, regions and styles. It’s a philosophy that the winery says celebrates curiosity, challenges convention and makes the most of the diversity of South Australia’s wine regions.

During her first two years with Alpha Box & Dice, McBryde has “immersed herself in the winery’s diverse portfolio, bringing her extensive experience and fresh perspective to its broad range of grape varieties and winemaking styles”.

“I’m super excited to continue and build on what’s been started,” she said.

“Wine is about people, place and fun. When you do all of those things, everything else just kind of falls into place.”

Vitis & Winemakers has expanded its New Zealand team with the appointment of two new product & sales managers and the promotion of Aimee McConway to office manager, “bringing additional hands-on winemaking, beverage and cellar experience to its growing commercial equipment business”.

Benjamin Alvano joins the business as product & sales manager, bringing international winemaking experience gained across Chile, Burgundy, Barolo and the Canary Islands.

The supplier said his practical cellar background provides a strong understanding of winemaking operations and the equipment required throughout production.

He is joined by Ben Murphy, also appointed product & sales manager. Murphy brings several years of hands-on cellar experience in Marlborough, adding practical local industry knowledge to the company’s sales and product support capabilities.

McConway, stepping into the role of office manager, has been with Vitis & Winemakers since 2023 across customer service, administration and accounts. Her new role encompasses the day-to-day coordination of the business and continued focus on customer service.

“We wanted to build a team that understands the equipment but also understands the environment it is being used in,” said Vitis & Winemakers managing director Paul Baggio.

“Having people with genuine cellar and winemaking experience is important because our customers are often looking for more than a product. They need to know that what they are considering will work in their operation.”

The company said the team expansion comes alongside the continued development of the Vitis & Winemakers online store, “which provides NZ wineries and beverage manufacturers with the largest range of commercial equipment, cellar equipment, processing equipment, parts and accessories”.

While smaller equipment, parts and accessories can be browsed and purchased online, the business “continues to provide direct support for larger equipment, Bucher Vaslin products, custom requirements and projects where selecting the right solution requires a more detailed discussion”.

“We are not trying to replace the relationship between wineries and their equipment suppliers with an online store,” Baggio said.

“The aim is to make it easier for customers to find and understand what is available, while retaining the industry knowledge and personal support that has always been important to us.”

More than 70 South Australian restaurants have become the first in the nation to be recognised by the world-renowned Michelin Guide, with a total of six winery-based restaurants receiving coveted Michelin stars.

Penfolds Magill Estate Restaurant was the only restaurant to receive two Michelin stars.

South Australia’s debut in the Michelin Guide marks the first time any Australian destination has been featured in the “global culinary bible”.

Premier Peter Malinauskas called it a historic moment for South Australia.

“The Michelin Guide puts South Australia on the world stage, showcasing our outstanding food, wine and hospitality to visitors from across the globe.

“It’s not just our chefs and restaurants — but the whole supply chain that makes our hospitality industry one of the best in the world, from our growers and producers to our winemakers and distillers and everyone in between.

“This global recognition will attract visitors to South Australia, creating jobs and supporting local businesses right across our visitor economy. We want people from all over the world to put South Australia on their travel itinerary, stay longer, spend more and discover everything our state has to offer,” he said.

Michelin Guide inspectors evaluated restaurants across the state through five universal criteria, including “the quality of the ingredients, the mastery of cooking techniques, the harmony of flavours, the personality of the cuisine and the overall consistency”.

The selection process is entirely independent, and restaurants cannot pay to be included or awarded distinctions.

Scott Huggins, director and chef of Magill Estate Restaurant at Penfolds, said that receiving two Michelin stars is an extraordinary honour and a proud moment for the team.

“What makes Magill Estate Restaurant unique is the experience we create for our guests.

“Our goal is to deliver something truly memorable through exceptional food, genuine hospitality and a deep connection to the location that surrounds us. This recognition is a testament to the passion, talent and dedication of our entire team.”

International director of the Michelin Guide, Gwendal Poullennec, called the state’s debut “very impressive”.

“What struck our Inspectors was the sheer diversity on display — European, Southeast Asian and Japanese traditions sitting naturally alongside native ingredients such as quandong, lemon myrtle and native Australian meats, never as novelty, but as an honest expression of place.

“From Adelaide’s easy-going dining rooms to the restaurants within wineries of the Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale, Clare Valley, and Adelaide Hills, fire is the thread that runs through it all — wood and charcoal used not as a trend, but as a technique that lets exceptional local produce speak for itself.

“It is a food culture unburdened by rigid tradition, and all the more distinctive for it — technically refined yet relaxed, generous and unmistakably South Australian in its warmth,” Poullennec said.

Minister for Tourism Emily Bourke congratulated the restaurants and chefs recognised in the first Michelin Guide South Australia.

“We know that many people around the world base their travel itineraries on MICHELIN Guide restaurants. This international recognition gives visitors another reason to book a trip to our state, and once they’re here, they’ll go onto experience even more of what South Australia has to offer.  “

The Michelin Guide website attracts more than 62 million visitors each year, in addition to the organisation’s 3.9 million Instagram followers and 3.8 million app users.

Approximately 4% (or 161 restaurants) of all starred restaurants in the Michelin Guide are rated three stars. There are 549 restaurants worldwide rated two Michelin stars.

At its annual general meeting today, Treasury Wine Estates (TWE) said it will highlight “early momentum” in its transformation agenda as it sharpens its focus on “leading brands and implements a simpler operating model to position the business for future growth”.

“We’ve taken decisive action over the past year to sharpen our focus on where we compete, the brands we invest in and how we operate. We’re already seeing stronger sales across our priority brands in key markets, and we’re determined to build on that progress,” CEO Sam Fischer said ahead of his first AGM for the company, a year after taking the helm at TWE.

“We’re optimistic about the long-term opportunity in the global wine category. We have some of the strongest brands in the world, from Penfolds and Matua to regional standouts like Wynns, Pepperjack, and Frank Family Vineyards. We’ll be investing more in them so they can reach their full potential with wine drinkers in established and emerging markets.”

TWE shared it will emphasise positive first quarter trading trends across its key markets, with growth across its priority brands:

  • China: Penfolds depletions growth slightly ahead of plan, supported by strong consumer demand
  • US: Stronger depletions growth across ‘Power Brands’, led by DAOU and Matua, and ‘Regional Heroes’
  • Australia: Depletions growth across ‘Power Brands’, led by Penfolds

The company said that, in China, Penfolds continues to perform strongly, “supported by strong consumer demand and the ongoing shift from parallel imports to authorised distribution channels”.

“Penfolds has built a reputation in China that extends well beyond wine — it’s recognised as a true luxury brand. We see significant opportunity to build on that strength, reaching more consumers, expanding our distribution and making Penfolds part of more occasions,” Fischer said.

In the US, TWE said its luxury wine portfolio has recorded three consecutive quarters of depletions growth, led by brands including DAOU and Frank Family Vineyards.

The conclusion of the first quarter also marks the transition to its new regional model, which aims to simplify operations and create clearer accountability in each market.

TWE shared it has also “made progress on the sale of non-priority brands and assets, including Seppelt, Rosemount, and vineyards, with approximately $50 million in proceeds confirmed to date”.

The company claimed these divestments complement the realisation of $40 million in cost benefits in F27 as part of the ‘Ascent transformation program’, which is “on track to realise $100 million in annual cost reductions by F29”.

At the AGM, the company will also reiterate its F27 earnings guidance, “with EBITS expected to be at least equivalent to F26, and its long-term EBITS margin target of 25%+”.

content:
The South Australian Government has revealed that there has been a significant increase in sales of SA wine to Canada and that it will build on this momentum with a new trade official to be based in Canada.

Nearly 18 months after several Canadian provinces pulled US wine from their shelves, Canada has emerged as a strong growth market, rising to become the state’s third largest wine export partner, overtaking the United States and behind only China and the United Kingdom.

Following “swift and targeted investment by the state government and local winemakers”, wine exports to Canada have grown by over $24 million in the year to August 2026, now valued at $128 million.

South Australia now accounts for 68 per cent of Australia’s total wine exports to Canada and exported 48.5 million litres of wine to Canada, up 38.6 per cent, in the year to August 2026.

Minister for State Development Chris Picton MP said the local wine industry quickly recognised an opportunity and moved quickly to get more wine on the shelves in Canada, “resulting in a major surge in sales through key Canadian retailers”.

“While the global wine market is undergoing a period of challenges and transition, it’s clear that South Australia remains well positioned for the future.

“By investing in these types of growth opportunities and leveraging the state’s unique ability to produce an exceptional diversity of quality wines, South Australia can continue to build a more sustainable and globally competitive future,” Minister Picton said.

Inca Lee, chief executive of the South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA), said the result demonstrates both the global reputation of SA wine and the agility of local winemakers.

“The state government’s investment through the Global Wine Growth Program has ensured South Australian wineries are visible and competitive in Canada at a time when retailers are looking for alternatives and consumers are willing to try something new.

“We know global conditions remain challenging and competition for consumers is intense, which is why continued investment in export market development and diversification remains so important,” she said.

Beginning in March 2025, many Canadian provinces including Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia removed US alcoholic beverages from liquor outlets and online platforms in response to tariffs imposed by the US.

To further support South Australian export opportunities to Canada, recruitment will soon start for the new trade official position to be based in Toronto. The position aims to help South Australian trade and investment across the country in opportunities such as food, wine, critical minerals and defence. Canada was previously served from South Australian trade officials in the United States.

The SA government said it has supported a series of retail promotions throughout Canada, which have seen an uplift in South Australian wine sales across the largest retailers in the country.

Recently, a four-week in-store promotion was held with the LCBO during July and August, featuring 16 South Australian wines – including Angove, Zonte’s Footsteps, Kilikanoon, Two Hands, and Bleasdale – across nine flagship stores, “resulting in a 49 per cent uplift in sales during the promotional period”.

Vigneron and director of Zonte’s Footstep, Brad Rey, said Canada has become a focus for the winery.

“Canada is a key market for Zonte’s Footstep, and with the support and focus of the South Australian Government on building awareness of the diversity and quality of South Australia’s wines, it has become a focal point across many provincial markets.

“We have benefited from this support immensely, with trade and consumers supporting our wines and experiencing strong sales amid the global pressures our industry is experiencing.”

Additionally, more than 75 South Australian wine in-store tasting events were held at BCLDB locations throughout the Canadian summer months.

Canada is an increasingly important strategic economic partner and is the state’s eighth largest export market with total SA goods exports to Canada valued at $575 million, an increase of 4.4 per cent.

Minister Picton recently discussed the growing opportunities in Canada with Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s Minister for Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade, while both at a major defence conference in Poland.

In addition, the FTA includes a dedicated ‘Annex on Trade in Wine, Whisky and Other Distilled Spirits’. NZW explained it aims to facilitate trade through “greater transparency, regulatory cooperation and clearer treatment of wine-specific issues” as well as establish “a working group on topics such as technical matters, labelling and certification”.

Improved access under the FTA is expected to make the market increasingly attractive to exporters. Depending on the wine’s value, tariffs on eligible New Zealand wine will reduce over ten years from 150% to either 50% or 25%.

New Zealand wine exports to India have “historically been modest, but they grew 48% in the last year to just under NZ$438,000”.

India’s wine market is largely concentrated in three cities: Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru. Together, those cities account for half of the country’s wine consumption and are home to around 70 million people. This is a market 13 times the size of New Zealand and is comparable to the United Kingdom.

Red wine accounts for a significant share of imported wine to India, “creating opportunities for a range of New Zealand wine styles alongside Sauvignon Blanc”. NZW said sales of wine are also growing. In the year to March 2026, Maharashtra (of which Mumbai is the capital city) sold a record 13 million litres, or around 1.4 million cases, while imports grew 14% by volume in 2025.

Together, the organisation believes these trends create a significant opportunity for New Zealand’s wine exporters.

“We thank Ministers and officials for their work to secure improved access to a market with considerable long-term potential”, said NZW CEO Anishka Jelicich.

“By working to bring the FTA into force quickly, the Government has ensured that New Zealand will also benefit from the Most Favoured Nation preferential tariff rates that have been negotiated under the EU India FTA. Those tariff reductions are more substantial and would not have been available to us if the EU deal had entered into force first.

“India remains largely untapped for New Zealand wine, so our focus is on helping our members assess the opportunity through practical market intelligence and insights, connections with key stakeholders and opportunities in-market to build their brands,” she said.

New Zealand Winegrowers recently hosted India’s only Master of Wine, Sonal C Holland, as a keynote speaker at its annual Wine Business Forum in Wellington. Her message to the audience was clear; the FTA removes a significant barrier, but long-term success in India will require commitment, patience and strong local relationships.

“Next month, we look forward to working with New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (NZTE) at ProWine Mumbai. The major international trade fair will include a 20 strong contingent of businesses showcasing New Zealand wine to the Indian trade. These types of events are incredibly valuable for our members, helping them to build distributor relationships and a pipeline in a growing premium segment,” said Jelicich.

content:
Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October and trophy winners announced Friday 13 November. Image supplied

More than 550 wines will be presented before the judges this week as tasting for the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show gets underway at Marlborough Events Centre.

From Wednesday 21 to Friday 23 October, chief judge Stu Marfell will be joined by shadow chief judge Murray Cook to lead a team of ten senior judges and six associate judges, including guest judges Jennifer Docherty MW from Hong Kong and long-time international wine judge Terry Copeland, through the tasting.

“We’re lucky to have two guest judges who bring real breadth to the table,” said Marfell.

“Jennifer has a truly global palate and a sharp sense of how Marlborough wines sit on the international stage, and Terry has been judging here and overseas for more than 30 years. Their perspective alongside the deep local knowledge of our panel is exactly the balance a regional show needs.”

Jennifer Docherty is one of around 420 Masters of Wine worldwide, and the first ethnically Chinese and Mandarin-speaking MW. Based in Hong Kong, she has spent more than 16 years as a wine buyer and educator across the UK, Hong Kong and mainland China. She now works as an educator, a judge and a wine communicator who has chaired a judging panel at the IWC Sake Competition in London for a decade.

Terry Copeland has judged wine competitions for more than three decades across New Zealand, London, San Francisco, Sydney and Tokyo. After a career in wine sales, marketing, export and supply chain, he went on to lead NZ Young Farmers and Federated Farmers, and is now Programme Director, Export Growth at the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Organisers said entries cover the full range of Marlborough wine styles, with growth in several classes this year. Sweet wine entries have almost doubled, the Sauvignon Blanc aged one year or older category is up and so is the current vintage regional blend Pinot Noir.

“It’s great to see more aged Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir coming through,” Marfell said.

“These styles work to showcase the depth and breadth Marlborough has to offer, as well as the confidence producers have in how their wines develop over time.”

The Legacy Trophy, which awards the wine with the highest scores for three vintages within a ten-year period, will be judged solely by the chief judges and guest judges today (20 October), before judging gets into full swing tomorrow.

QuayConnect is once again the show’s naming sponsor with general manager Jaron McLeod saying the company is proud to continue its support.

“Marlborough wine is one of the top of the south’s great export stories, and much of it moves through our supply chain on its way to the world,” he said.

“Backing a show that recognises the skill and care that goes into every bottle is a natural fit for QuayConnect.”

Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October, with trophy winners announced at the Marlborough Wine Show Celebration on Friday 13 November 2026.

Every day we work with what the region and our own gardens give us, and to have that recognised by The Age Good Food Guide means a great deal to every one of us,” he said.

First published in 1979, The Age Good Food Guide “remains the benchmark for dining in Victoria”.

summary:

content:
The second installation of a two-part opinion piece by Edward Cavanagh that concludes a cautionary tale: understanding what motivated China to adopt the position it did in relation to Australia, and how the subsequent fight played out, should dampen any optimism about the re-emergence of the Chinese market for the wine industry.

In 2019, China was Australia’s largest trading partner, representing more than a quarter of its total trade balance. And Australian wines made up a small but significant chunk of this figure, accounting for over a billion dollars’ worth of exports per year.

A great market had opened up.

But then a great market would disappear – and the importance of certain positions adopted by the Australian government in this saga should be highlighted.

“A market of over a billion dollars per annum became a market of a few hundred thousand bucks per maybe-once-every-now-and-then-let’s-see.”

 

We poked the panda

The Australia-China relationship had episodically experienced some stress-testing throughout 2018 and 2019, the biggest years of climbing export growth for the wine industry, over a number of issues. These included statements made by Foreign Minister Julie Bishop between March and July of 2018 about maritime security in the South China Sea, followed by the federal government’s announcement (and only the day before Turnbull was ousted) on August 23rd 2018 that Huawei’s 5G network would not be approved for rollout in Australia. There were also repeated allegations from late 2017 right up to mid-2019 of government interference (mostly through some pretty questionable political donations and a number of reports that Chinese spies had been planted in parliaments and universities).

But the real deterioration of the relationship came with the outbreak of COVID-19 and Prime Minister Scott Morrison’s early response to the pandemic.

Specifically, the People’s Republic of China took offence to a series of public announcements by Morrison throughout April and May of 2020, which were reiterated in a speech before the UN General Assembly in September 2020, about the need for an independent probe into the Chinese origins of the COVID-19 outbreak. This involved providing the World Health Organisation with what Morrison called ‘weapons inspector-style powers’ in Wuhan. Throughout these months of lockdown and uncertainty, Morrison arrogated to himself the responsibility of engaging in something of a diplomatic campaign by zoom conference, in which he attempted to drum up international support for an intervention by calling into question the truthfulness of Chinese reporting about the outbreak and its early spread – remarks that he was unafraid to make repeatedly in press conferences in Australia at this time.

Whatever the clarity or the opacity of the reporting of Chinese health authorities about the outbreak of coronavirus, Morrison’s COVID-19 campaign came a little too close, for the PRC’s liking, to an allegation of responsibility for the global economic turmoil that the pandemic had wrought.

When, in August 2020, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce announced that it would be investigating the impact of current trading arrangements on the economy, Australia’s diplomatic lines to China had already run cold. It did not help that, within just weeks of the Chinese investigation into trade getting up and running, the Australian government resolved to join a UN chorus in condemning China’s treatment of Muslim Uyghurs in Xinjiang and political dissidents in Hong Kong.

Confirming a provisional decision reached in November 2020, which came in the context of a few knee-jerk quarantine restrictions, a formal announcement followed from Beijing on March 26th 2021 that the export market for Australian wine was no more.

But the imposition of trade barriers at the Chinese end did not simply come through a new blanket tariff, as Angus Colovic has explained in his treatment of the topic. The official determination by the Chinese Ministry of Commerce found that Australian exporters had been guilty of ‘dumping’ their wines into the Chinese market.

Now this was World Trade Organization parlance for the practice of undercutting domestic producers through unfair competitive advantage. Whatever the increase in area under vine that China witnessed in these years, it was hardly the case that the Chinese grape and wine sector had grown to become anywhere near the size of Australia’s, or any other of the many nations who sought entry into this lucrative market, leaving aside whatever their own regulations permitted around quality and blending material for Chinese-produced wines for its domestic market.

Still, the logic of the determination was clear enough. And it was expressed in a way that all of the trade lawyers could well understand as they licked their lips, even if they disagreed about the consistency of this decision with the general tenor of entire libraries full of WTO general agreements. Whatever they could or could not do about it, the reality was that China’s anti-dumping laws kicked in with immediate effect. Even with ships on the water, they kicked in. Overnight, the duties imposed on Australian wine in containers of 2L or less landed anywhere between 116% and 218%, with the earliest reports indicating a blanket imposition of 200%. The dragon had snorted.

There are two striking features when it came to the imposition of these duties. One was the sheer scale of them. The other was the abrupt rapidity of them. And Australian wines were suddenly and immediately nowhere near capable of reaching the Chinese market at a competitive price point as a result of them.

Some of this wine had to be discounted to achieve at least some return; a lot of it was warehoused; a bit of it went into the black market; a good deal of it just sat on cargo ships destined either to return to Australia for relabelling or otherwise disposal. Some shipping insurers paid out; others didn’t.

A disaster like this only had one parallel in history: and that is when the UK had rather hastened to join the European Economic Community in 1973 without forewarning any of their Commonwealth trading partners about the consequences that this would inevitably entail for supply chains that had been mostly linked up in the Victorian era. Quantitatively, the scale of the volte face in China was of much greater magnitude than this, however. Millions of litres were destined for the Chinese market. And overnight this wine needed to find another home – mostly, alas, in storage. A market of over a billion dollars per annum became a market of a few hundred thousand bucks per maybe-once-every-now-and-then-let’s-see.

These measures targeted bottled wine.

Altogether separately, but around the same time, the movement of bulk wine into and around China was subject to new customs regulations, which required registration, more paperwork, compliance to new standards, and stricter labelling requirements, in addition to new restrictions imposed on the receiving entity.

In other words, whereas Australian bottled wine was priced out of the Chinese market through tariffs, Australian bulk wine could only ever make it into an increasingly competitive market wrapped in layers of red tape that meant higher costs and greater uncertainty both for exporters and importers.

Widely seen as a retaliation against the Morrison government’s remarks about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic, there are other facets to the Chinese loosening of its embrace of Australian wine that are probably worth considering in a way that isn’t unhelpfully woebegone.

Such facets should certainly mitigate against any optimistic belief that the Chinese market for Australian wine will somehow magically return someday soon to the glory years of 2016–2020, and should probably have mitigated against the uninhibited optimism that was shown towards the foreverness of the market in the first place.

For starters, Chinese people were beginning to drink less in this period. And per capita alcohol consumption in China has continued to fall ever since. White collar professionals in the cities were simply no longer totally writing themselves off at work events as they once did. Lavish banquets were already apparently becoming less frequent even before coronavirus. What’s more, cultures around gift-giving were also beginning to shift. Bottles of big red wine with big red labels became big red flags. Little and little remained in this world apart from a reverence for fine wine more so as a cake to have rather than a cake to eat. Penfolds would always do well in this market; Penfolds counterfeits would surprisingly do even better. Aside from luxury wines, what Australia had been flooding the Chinese market with were cheapish big-bodied red wines, sometimes with more than a bit of residual sugar, and which were sometimes bottled up with labels all flashy with orientalist iconography – and these were only ever going to enjoy a temporary moment in the rising sun with so much of this new sociocultural smog settling into the cityscape.

If history is anything to go by, then Australian wine exporters would eventually have discovered this for themselves, albeit far too late, and then instinctively geared themselves up to discount their ways out of trouble, like they did with just about every other market crisis. But in China they never got the chance. Its government’s anti-dumping measures, which are still widely seen by analysts and commentators as an exertion of China’s power of economic coercion, caught everyone off-guard.

“And I rather hope that some of the marketing masterminds who are paid by winery businesses, like those who are paid out of industry levies, consider more fulsomely the geopolitical context of the world that was shaken up by the Global Financial Crisis of 2008-2010 before they plug into any overseas market again, let alone a market so fickle, tricky, twisted, and cunning as China’s.”

 

Enter the trade lawyers

Australia put up a fight using the World Trade Organization (WTO) dispute settlement system.

The first step required Australia to invite China to participate in bilateral negotiations for sixty days, which it did on June 22nd, 2021. But since there was no agreement at the end of this period, Australia was entitled to ask the WTO Dispute Settlement Board (DSB) to establish a panel to consider whether or not arbitration was appropriate. In the meantime, both parties, China and Australia, made it clear that they wished to advance their own cases in this forum, and agreed to a common procedure for arbitration in December 2021. When a new standalone panel was established in March 2022, both of the parties overloaded it with ‘voluminous evidence’, such that an extension had to be agreed to the process.

And then even more evidence kept rolling in!

Come August, the Chair of the panel had to report to the DSB that the evidence was indeed so ‘voluminous’ that a determination would not be delivered in 2022. A month later, the Chair clarified that in fact the panel did not expect to issue a report to the parties before mid-2023.

That brings us to October 30th, 2023, when the Chair of the panel informed the DSB that the panel report was finished and scheduled to be circulated to Members on November 10th, 2023. But no report was ever delivered because, on the same day, the Chinese team and the Australian team announced that they were in a position to settle the dispute away from the WTO, and therefore jointly requested the panel to suspend its work until March 31st, 2024.

That’s right, a two-year-long exercise in paying for lawyers to develop a complex argument over 46 separate articles of the WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement, 38 separate articles of the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, and even four articles of the true classic in the multilateral genre, the General Agreement on Tariffs Trade, resulted in thousands of pages of evidence about the wine trade but no report.

That the Australian submissions were overwhelmingly more serious, and likelier to earn a determination in Australia’s favour, seems a reasonable enough conclusion to reach. Unwishful of attracting any further political attention towards their strategies of economic coercion that were becoming increasingly notorious on the world stage, the PRC did not want a ruling that could jeopardise any of its activities here and elsewhere, current or planned; it wanted a deal. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was invited to Beijing for talks with President Xi Jinping in early November 2023, and wine was right at the top of the agenda, above even lobsters, visas, and iron ore.

Few people can entirely know what goes behind closed doors of this kind, but it seems plausible that Albanese received assurances from Xi Jinping that China would restart imports of lobster and review the tariffs on wine, if in return Australia committed to a formal withdrawal of its case before the WTO panel.

This outcome was confirmed, when, on March 29th, 2024, both parties announced to the WTO that they were discontinuing their case. Later, on June 17th, 2024 – three and a half years after the provisional ban on Australian imports of bottled wine was announced – a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade of Australia was signed in Canberra and Beijing.

“The Chinese government’s anti-dumping measures, which are still widely seen by analysts and commentators as an exertion of China’s power of economic coercion, caught everyone off guard.”

 

Open sesame…again?

China was open for trading again.

But there was a problem.

Citizens of the PRC never rediscovered their appetite for Australian wines after 2025 to the extent they were quaffing them before 2021.

One wonders whether or not it would have been better for the wine industry to have seen a WTO determination instead of this outcome. Alas, it does not matter now.

The point to remember here, and in the context of the findings presented in my previous article on this topic, is that Australia was outdone. And I rather hope that some of the marketing masterminds who are paid by winery businesses, like those who are paid out of industry levies, consider more fulsomely the geopolitical context of the world that was shaken up by the Global Financial Crisis of 2008-2010 before they plug into any overseas market again, let alone a market so fickle, tricky, twisted, and cunning as China’s.

As with sundry other Chinese experiments that involve playing around with foreign economies, the PRC has played such a beautiful long game over the past two decades. They are arguably the only ones who know how to mix economic coercion with diplomatic mind-games to play one convincingly, and the sheer size of their market, coupled with the supreme level of control the PRC enjoys over its own institutions, provide them a commanding power to dominate whenever they choose to play it.

Australian wine was but a pawn, but it is unlikely to have had any role at all in the Chinese masterplan were it not for the Hawke-era reforms on tariffs, tax, and industry protections that were responsible for putting the sector into exactly this position.

I am not for a moment suggesting that those reforms were a bad thing. They were right for the time and right for Australia.

Still, we are allowed to feel upset by the ways in which globalisation and free trade were sold to neoliberal economies on a set of presumptions that China, through its might and power, has subsequently unsettled; one might also pause in this frame to consider equally the EU’s subsidy system, New Zealand’s eligibility for WET rebates, and the Trump tariff regime, alongside Chinese economic coercion, and reconvene with the same scepticism.

If free trade supposes an openly competitive arena whereby everyone takes their cues from the market, then the experience of the Australian wine industry both at home and abroad, and especially when it comes to China, shows that this arrangement has not always played out all that reciprocally or fairly. Australia got smashed, but it did not impose massive reverse tariffs on Chinese goods coming into Australia; it took the principled route instead to the WTO. What it got was four years of uncertainty, and the re-emergence of a market that was hardly as big or as lucrative for the vast majority of producers as it was before the walls came down.

No export-oriented national wine industry should ever place all of its eggs into this basket again, but South Africa recently has, and others probably will.

Australia looks like it might again too. But should it?

content:
Rachel McBryde has taken over the role following Sam Berketa’s ten-year tenure. Image supplied.

For the first time in a decade, McLaren Vale winery Alpha Box & Dice has a new head winemaker.

Rachel McBryde, who joined the business in 2024, steps into the role following Sam Berketa’s ten-year tenure, bringing “international experience, a passion for lesser-known varieties and a fresh perspective to its ever-evolving Alphabet of Wine”.

Her career has taken her around the world, from Marlborough in New Zealand to Napa Valley and Ontario in North America. McBryde also spent five years working across d’Arenberg and Gemtree in McLaren Vale, explored sparkling winemaking in the Adelaide Hills and spent three years in Coonawarra at Katnook Estate and Penley Estate, working with some of Australia’s most celebrated Cabernet Sauvignon.

“What drew me to Alpha Box & Dice was a love of the weird and wonderful,” said McBryde.

“The Alphabet of Wine and its focus on lesser-known varieties is something that really interests me. In Australia, we have this incredible freedom to grow varieties from Burgundy alongside those from Piedmont or the Mosel and develop our own interpretations of what those grapes can be in a new environment. That’s exciting, and it’s what we do at Alpha Box & Dice.”

Built around the idea of creating an entire ‘Alphabet of Wine’, Alpha Box & Dice approaches each letter as a different winemaking project, exploring new varieties, regions and styles. It’s a philosophy that the winery says celebrates curiosity, challenges convention and makes the most of the diversity of South Australia’s wine regions.

During her first two years with Alpha Box & Dice, McBryde has “immersed herself in the winery’s diverse portfolio, bringing her extensive experience and fresh perspective to its broad range of grape varieties and winemaking styles”.

“I’m super excited to continue and build on what’s been started,” she said.

“Wine is about people, place and fun. When you do all of those things, everything else just kind of falls into place.”

Vitis & Winemakers has expanded its New Zealand team with the appointment of two new product & sales managers and the promotion of Aimee McConway to office manager, “bringing additional hands-on winemaking, beverage and cellar experience to its growing commercial equipment business”.

Benjamin Alvano joins the business as product & sales manager, bringing international winemaking experience gained across Chile, Burgundy, Barolo and the Canary Islands.

The supplier said his practical cellar background provides a strong understanding of winemaking operations and the equipment required throughout production.

He is joined by Ben Murphy, also appointed product & sales manager. Murphy brings several years of hands-on cellar experience in Marlborough, adding practical local industry knowledge to the company’s sales and product support capabilities.

McConway, stepping into the role of office manager, has been with Vitis & Winemakers since 2023 across customer service, administration and accounts. Her new role encompasses the day-to-day coordination of the business and continued focus on customer service.

“We wanted to build a team that understands the equipment but also understands the environment it is being used in,” said Vitis & Winemakers managing director Paul Baggio.

“Having people with genuine cellar and winemaking experience is important because our customers are often looking for more than a product. They need to know that what they are considering will work in their operation.”

The company said the team expansion comes alongside the continued development of the Vitis & Winemakers online store, “which provides NZ wineries and beverage manufacturers with the largest range of commercial equipment, cellar equipment, processing equipment, parts and accessories”.

While smaller equipment, parts and accessories can be browsed and purchased online, the business “continues to provide direct support for larger equipment, Bucher Vaslin products, custom requirements and projects where selecting the right solution requires a more detailed discussion”.

“We are not trying to replace the relationship between wineries and their equipment suppliers with an online store,” Baggio said.

“The aim is to make it easier for customers to find and understand what is available, while retaining the industry knowledge and personal support that has always been important to us.”
